name: Beard vitamins (zinc, B-complex, D)

lead: Beard-growth stacks combine zinc, B-complex vitamins (often biotin) and vitamin D, aiming for a thicker, healthier-looking beard by making sure follicles are not short of key nutrients.

Zinc, biotin and other B vitamins take part in skin and hair biology, and deficiency is associated with hair changes: zinc deficiency with thin, sparse hair, and rare biotin deficiency with thinning. Reference sources report no randomized trials showing biotin helps hair in healthy people, and no studies were found on these vitamins for beard growth.

paras: They are taken as over-the-counter multivitamin-style pills or capsules, usually daily alongside a normal diet and other beard care. People who fix a real shortfall may notice change over several months as hair cycles turn over.

Biotin at 5 mg per day or more can distort thyroid and vitamin D lab results. Very high vitamin D intake can cause toxicity with high blood calcium. US supplements are not approved for effectiveness before sale.

angle.text: Correcting nutrient shortfalls supports healthier follicles and hair, which is the route to a thicker-looking beard. Zinc and biotin deficiencies are linked to thin hair; trials of extra vitamins for beard growth specifically were not found.

lead: Beard-growth stacks sold or discussed online often combine zinc, B-complex vitamins (frequently biotin) and vitamin D. Deficiencies of some of these nutrients are associated with hair changes: zinc deficiency with thin, sparse hair, and biotin deficiency, which is rare, with hair thinning.[1][2]

Reference sources report that there are no randomized controlled trials proving biotin supplementation helps healthy people's hair, and general hair-loss references state that dietary supplements are not typically recommended.[1][3] No studies found address these vitamins specifically for beard growth.
infobox: Zinc, biotin and other B vitamins, vitamin D

paras: Zinc deficiency is described as causing alopecia ("thin and sparse hair"), skin problems and impaired taste or smell.[2] Biotin deficiency is rare in people eating a normal diet, and mild cases can cause hair thinning, brittle nails or a facial rash; most cases arise from a genetic condition, biotinidase deficiency.[1] Iron and vitamin B12 deficiencies are listed among less common causes of hair loss.[3]

Biotin supplements of 5 mg/day or more can interfere with immunoassays used for thyroid hormones and vitamin D levels, giving falsely normal or abnormal results; a 2017 FDA safety communication on this is cited.[1] Vitamin D toxicity is rare but occurs with high-dose supplements, causing high blood calcium; the US tolerable upper intake for adults is 4,000 IU/day.[4]
In the US supplements are not required to be approved for effectiveness before sale, and labels may carry structure/function claims with a disclaimer that the FDA has not evaluated them.[1]
No studies found for beard growth. Related general information: a review cited by Wikipedia found no randomized trials showing biotin supplementation helps hair in healthy people.[1]
